newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian meat's trading edge seen hit by fees.
newsitem.headline: Australian meat's trading edge seen hit by fees.

text.p: Increased inspection charges by the Australian Quarantine and Inspection Service (AQIS) would deal a major blow to the Australian meat industry's ability to compete internationally, the industry said on Wednesday.
The Federal government plans to charge the meat industry fully for the operation of AQIS, which previously received an annual A$14.5 million government payment.

Increased fees of more than 300 percent being demanded by AQIS from industry would have an adverse impact on Australia's meat export industry, which was already under strain, the chief executive officer of the National Meat Association of Australia,
David Abba, and the executive director of the Australian Meat Council, Christopher Creal, said in a statement.
AQIS proposed to raise registration fees for export establishments across the board to fund its A$72 million a year cost of operation, they said.
Some registration fees would rise to A$6,000 from A$1,500 a year while others would rise to A$14,000 from A$3,500 a year, they said.

Some export processors would face an increase in registration fees to a new high of A$33,000 from A$8,280, while export slaughter houses faced a fee increase to A$122,000 a year from A$30,350, they said.
Area technical managers, who are currently funded by the government, would suddenly cost meat processors A$1,300 a day or A$200 an hour, they said.
The President of the Cattle Council of Australia, John Wyld, said he was dismayed with the decision and would be urging the government to keep current charges in place until the issue was resolved.
